name: Human Interpreters for Sensitive Meetings
title: Human Interpreters for Sensitive Meetings
answer: Some school conversations are too consequential for machine translation. Meetings about special education, discipline, health, safety, or a child's wellbeing require a qualified human interpreter, while machine translation may be suitable for routine exchanges. The idea matters because poor interpretation can damage families' access to services and their trust in schools.

sections.body: This idea draws a clear line between routine communication and sensitive meetings. Machine translation can help with casual conversation, such as a teacher speaking with a parent at pickup. But when a family must understand their rights and make decisions, a qualified human interpreter should be used. The problem it solves is the risk that poor interpretation will keep families from special education services and weaken their trust in schools. District policy should make that distinction explicit so staff know which tool or service fits the situation.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In practice, a teacher might use Microsoft Translator on a phone for a brief, routine chat with a parent at pickup. For meetings about special education, discipline, health, safety, or a child's wellbeing, the school should arrange a qualified human interpreter instead. The text does not give separate grade bands, so the same distinction applies across grade levels. Districts should keep a list of contracted interpreters and make booking them easy for staff. Staff should plan ahead so the right interpreter is available when a sensitive meeting is scheduled.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The book does not attach an evidence label to this idea. It cites research with Spanish, Portuguese, and Cantonese speaking families, finding that poor interpretation reduced their access to special education services and their trust in schools (Tang Yan, 2022). The text adds that those harms are hard to undo. No other study, figure, or finding is given.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: Machine translation should not be used for meetings where a family must understand rights and make decisions. The text warns that using a family member, especially a child, as an interpreter for sensitive meetings should be avoided. A child should not have to interpret news about their own discipline or disability to their parents. The choice to book a qualified human interpreter for these conversations stays with school staff and district policy, not with a translation tool. Planning ahead is the safeguard that makes the right support possible.
